content: Meloxicam is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) primarily used to manage pain associated with arthritis. For osteoarthritis, the standard oral dose is 15 mg daily, but a reduced dose of 7.5 mg is recommended for older patients to minimize potential risks. This review aimed to assess the effectiveness and safety of oral meloxicam in managing acute postoperative pain. The evaluation was based on clinical studies involving patients with established postoperative pain, with outcomes measured primarily over a six-hour period using standardized methods. This type of study design has been a long-standing approach to confirm the analgesic properties of medications. The objective of this review was to determine the efficacy of a single oral dose of meloxicam in relieving acute postoperative pain and to identify any associated adverse events. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including Cochrane CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Oxford Pain Relief Database, up to June 2009. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials that evaluated oral meloxicam for the relief of acute postoperative pain in adults. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted relevant data. The planned analysis involved calculating the proportion of participants who experienced at least 50% pain relief over a 4to 6-hour period using validated methods. Additional outcomes included the number needed to treat to benefit (NNT), the proportion of participants requiring rescue analgesia, the time to rescue analgesia, and data on adverse events and withdrawals. However, the search did not identify any studies that specifically examined the use of oral meloxicam in patients with established postoperative pain. As a result, there is currently no evidence to support the efficacy of oral meloxicam for this indication. The authors concluded that, in the absence of such evidence, the use of oral meloxicam for acute postoperative pain cannot be justified. Furthermore, since there are no trials demonstrating its analgesic efficacy in basic acute pain studies, its use for other indications should be approached with caution. Given the wide availability of alternative drugs within the same class, there is no pressing need for further research on this specific application of meloxicam.
